messages.content: Cual va a ser el clima en la cdmx?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning:
The user asks "Cual va a ser el clima en la cdmx?" which translates to "What will be the weather in Mexico City?" They want current weather forecast. We need to use the Open-Meteo API. The tool requires us to call requests_get with appropriate parameters.

We need to find the latitude and longitude of CDMX. Mexico City coordinates: approximately 19.4326° N, -99.1332° W. So latitude=19.4326, longitude=-99.1332.

We can query the Open-Meteo API for current weather. According to Open-Meteo documentation, we can use the endpoint: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=...&longitude=...&current_weather=true

We might also want to specify timezone. But not necessary.

So we call the function with url: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast", params: {latitude: 19.4326, longitude: -99.1332, current_weather: true}. The function signature expects params as an object with keys: latitude, longitude, elevation. It doesn't mention current_weather. But maybe we can pass it anyway. The function signature only includes latitude, longitude, elevation. But we can add other query parameters? The description says "Query parameters for the GET request." It lists latitude, longitude, elevation. But we can still pass others. However, the function signature may restrict to those keys. But we can try passing current_weather: true. Let's see if the function signature allows arbitrary keys. It says "params: // Query parameters for the GET request. { ... }". It lists latitude, longitude, elevation. It doesn't list current_weather. But we can still pass it. The function might accept additional keys. But it's safer to just pass the known ones. But we need to get current weather. The Open-Meteo API uses "current_weather=true" parameter. So we need to pass that. The function signature might allow arbitrary keys. Let's assume we can pass it.

Thus we call:

{
